You're producing a ~80s Nxeon product commercial by hand-authoring Remotion/TSX scenes and pushing them to the `baz` CLI (Bazaar video tool) via its TOKEN-FREE authoring path. Nxeon is a VPS/hosting/game-server platform (nxeon.cloud), codebase at /opt/nxeon.

## ABSOLUTE HARD RULES — READ FIRST, THESE OVERRIDE EVERYTHING ELSE
1. **NEVER call `baz prompt` for ANY reason.** That is Baz's server-side AI scene-generation path and it spends real account balance. The user explicitly said, minutes ago: "you spent credits on baz when you werent supposed to... do not spend credits on baz." A prior agent violated this by using `baz prompt` and it cost $4.17 without proper approval — do not repeat that mistake. You write 100% of the TSX yourself, by hand, following the skill spec below. If you are ever tempted to reach for `baz prompt` because hand-authoring is hard, STOP and report back to me instead — do not take the shortcut.
2. **NEVER call `baz export start`.** That is the one billable step in this whole workflow. When everything is authored, validated (`baz project validate`), and preview-checked (`baz preview`), STOP THERE. Report back to me (your parent session) with what you built and a preview description. Do not export. I will get explicit human approval separately before that step ever runs.
3. If ANY command you need to run shows a nonzero cost in `baz balance --pricing` (media upload, transcription, anything), STOP and report back before running it rather than assuming it's fine. Only the free-tier commands listed below are pre-approved: `baz project create`, `baz context add`, `baz scenes create --file`, `baz scenes set-code --file`, `baz scenes positions`, `baz project validate`, `baz preview`, `baz review`, `baz balance` / `baz balance --pricing` (read-only checks are fine).
4. This skill's format is **music-led, no voiceover** — so you should not need any TTS/voice generation spend at all. Good, keep it that way; do not add a voiceover track.

## Setup
```bash
npm i -g bazaar.it@latest
baz --version
baz auth status
```
If not authenticated, STOP and report back — do not guess credentials.

## The skill you're implementing (verbatim spec — follow its exact motion grammar, timing, and physics)

Title: Claude Design Ad — Format: Landscape 1920×1080 @ 30fps, ~80s, 31 scenes, ALL on track 0 (single track — `baz scenes create` puts each on its own track by default; fix with one `baz scenes positions --apply` call carrying track/start/duration for every scene once they're all created). No voiceover, music-led, cut to the beat. Every scene hand-written TSX, zero generation tokens. One shared kit (colors/type/easing constants) duplicated verbatim into every scene file so values crossing a scene boundary are byte-identical. Author in real 1920×1080 pixel space, never scale up from 720.

Beat map (9 patterns, in order): cold-open → generate → status-lockup → app-reveal → ui-interaction → montage-wall → artifact-swap → handoff → brand-ident. (status-lockup repeats multiple short times between the bigger beats as "punctuation" — that's part of why there are 31 scenes total, not 9.)

**cold-open**: Wordmark centred on canvas. Cursor enters, hovers → soft pill appears behind it. Pill MORPHS into a composer/input box: pill rect → card rect, background color shift, wordmark letters drain left-to-right as the card takes over. Morph is LINEAR over ~7 frames (no easing). Placeholder text types in, toolbar glyphs appear one by one, then real prompt text types. Ends darkening toward the next beat's background.

**generate**: Composer holds, then pushes back (hold → commit, not continuous drift) while the artifact/result grows behind it. Attachment-style chips pop in above the input as context. Cursor travels to a Send/Deploy button, presses; the input card fades; the artifact takes the frame. The artifact BUILDS (pieces arriving in sequence) — never fades in as one complete thing.

**status-lockup**: Full-bleed canvas, brand mark + a single italic present-tense gerund typing in with an animated ellipsis ("Provisioning…", "Booting…", "Securing…" — vary the verb each repeat). Pill sized to the FULL final word up front, not the in-progress typed length (else it resizes mid-type and clips letters). Short: 0.9–1.7s each. These are punctuation between bigger beats, not scenes in their own right.

**app-reveal**: Window chrome assembles in stagger, not simultaneous: tab bar → left rail → content canvas → floating toolbar. The content area has its OWN coordinate origin (window x/y + rail width + tab-bar height) — anything positioned against it must account for that offset or it lands hundreds of px off; this is the single most common bug, watch for it.

**ui-interaction**: The credibility core of the whole film — real cursor operating a real UI. ONE cursor design for the entire film (plain arrow, white outline, dark fill) — never swap cursor shapes between beats. Click legibility = a brief ring-pulse at the cursor tip + a small press-dip, not a different cursor. Anchor the cursor INSIDE the element it clicks (a zero-size wrapper in that element's own coordinate space) so it tracks reflow/scale for free — never position the cursor in raw frame coordinates, that desyncs the moment a layout shifts. Cursor physics are ballistic: launch fast, decelerate hard, then hold dead still, ~11 frames, `out(poly(4))` easing. A good measured travel profile across those 11 frames: `1020px → 140 → 20 → 3 → 0` (i.e. most of the distance covers in the first couple frames, then a hard settle) — linear drift is the #1 tell that kills realism, avoid it. One continuous motion from scene start, never idle-then-jump. Every click must cause a VISIBLE consequence in the same beat (a value changes, a panel opens, a status flips, a toast confirms) — a click with no effect reads as broken. Drags: the dragged value follows the cursor 1:1, untouched controls stay perfectly still (no ambient wobble on anything else). Hide the cursor once its interaction is done, don't let it linger. Any highlighted/active state must be earned by a preceding interaction, never just appear.

**montage-wall**: A drifting grid of tile cards showing breadth. HORIZONTAL drift only — per-row vertical drift at different rates makes rows converge/overlap and looks like a bug. Tiles are real UI screenshots (thin browser-chrome bar on each so they read as captured software, not flat gradient cards — flat cards read as unfinished/empty). Need a pool of ≥19 distinct tiles for a 24–63 cell grid, indexed with a modulus coprime to the column count so repeats don't line up in the same row. Resolve OUT of the wall by camera whip (2–4 frames onto the target tile, which IS one of the wall tiles, not a separately-grown card) — never resolve by fade. Entering the wall: the prior scene must finish before the wall arrives (~2 frame overlap max) — a long cross-dissolve reads as muddy double-exposure.

**artifact-swap**: An artifact arrives with a small overshoot-settle, HOLDS, gets edited via some control, then whip-pushes into a detail view at the end. A comment/edit control types a request, is submitted, and the artifact visibly changes on that beat. Scale elements with CSS `transform` only, never by animating width/height/font-size directly (that causes text reflow/rewrap every frame and reads as jitter) — keep artifacts at a fixed layout size and scale the wrapper instead.

**handoff**: An export/share-style menu cascades open item by item (pop, not fade), cursor walks the list snapping row to row, background artifact cross-fades through variants behind it. Ends on a real command/code block with a clicked confirm action ("Copy" → "Copied") to motivate the cut.

**brand-ident**: Final two beats. First, a callback to the cold-open lockup (same mark, same position) with a tracked-in attribution/tagline line. Then the actual brand ident: mark pops in with overshoot, wordmark wipes on, long hold to close.

## Adapt this arc to Nxeon — here's the story mapping

The film's arc is: *a promise typed → an artifact generated → tweaked through real UI interaction → many artifacts shown → handed off → brand ident.* For Nxeon, the "artifact" is **a live server**, and the product surface is the deploy wizard / server dashboard, not a design tool. Map it like this:

1. **cold-open**: "NXEON" wordmark on a deep navy canvas → cursor hovers → pill morphs into the deploy composer (a plan/OS picker input). Placeholder "Deploy a server..." types in, then a real prompt-style flow: user "picks" a plan.
2. **generate**: The deploy composer commits, cursor clicks "Deploy". The composer card fades, a server dashboard builds itself piece by piece behind it (this IS the app-reveal content, can blend directly into #4).
3. **status-lockup** (repeat 3-4x through the film as punctuation): "Provisioning…", "Booting…", "Securing…", "Live." — brand mark + italic gerund, full-bleed navy.
4. **app-reveal**: The real Nxeon server dashboard chrome assembles — tab bar, left rail (Overview/Console/Backups/etc.), content canvas, floating action toolbar. RECREATE this as real TSX matching Nxeon's actual dashboard, using the reference screenshots below — don't invent a generic admin panel, build the real one.
5. **ui-interaction** (this is the important one — the user specifically asked for cursor-driven interaction with a recreated real UI): the cursor operates the actual dashboard — clicks a power/restart button and status flips, clicks into settings and a value changes, clicks a "47 seconds" timer/stat that ticks to completion. Every click has a visible on-screen consequence, per the pattern above.
6. **montage-wall**: grid of tiles showing Nxeon's breadth — recreated screenshots of: the deploy wizard, Matrix (AI app builder, showing 6 parallel app-build panels), business email inbox, one-click WordPress install, the free Minecraft dashboard, the paid game-server catalog. Include the user's own real Minecraft gameplay clip (path below) as one of the "tiles" — if Baz's tile/media system in this skill's TSX approach supports a `<video>` element inside a tile card (it should, since Remotion TSX can embed a `<video>` or `<OffthreadVideo>` tag pointing at an uploaded media asset), use the real clip there; if you determine video-in-tile genuinely isn't feasible in this skill's grid layout, use a freeze-frame from the clip as a static tile image instead and say so in your report — don't silently skip it.
7. **artifact-swap**: the Matrix beat — an app spec is typed/edited, and multiple app-build panels visibly update in response (swap-edit pattern, not fade).
8. **handoff**: an export-style menu (or a "connect your domain" / "get started" menu) cascades open, cursor walks it, ends on a real command block (e.g. a `ssh root@your-server` or a deploy CLI snippet) with a clicked "Copy" → "Copied" confirm.
9. **brand-ident**: callback to the cold-open NXEON wordmark with the tagline "First month free on shared hosting. Deploy today at nxeon.cloud." then the final brand ident hold.

## Nxeon brand facts — use ONLY these, never invent numbers or claims
- Palette (exact, don't eyeball or substitute): deep navy background `#0a0e1a` → `#0f1420` (use as a gradient range), violet accent `#6f47f5` (secondary `#8b5cf6`), cyan/blue accent `#3b82f6` and `#06b6d4`. Gradients in the real product go `from-accent-blue/90 to-brand-500/90` — mirror that violet→blue gradient direction for buttons/accents. This is a dark-canvas brand (NOT the skill's default cream canvas) — invert the cold-open/brand-ident background patterns to navy instead of cream, keep the rest of the motion grammar identical.
- "Your server is 47 seconds away" / "online in 47 seconds" — real, live marketing copy (app/page.tsx). Use exactly "47 seconds", nothing else.
- "99.9% uptime SLA" — real, live copy. Not 99%.
- Matrix: Nxeon's AI app builder, connects directly to a customer's own server, builds up to 6 apps at once with AI.
- Business email = real mailbox hosting. One-click WordPress installs are real.
- Free Minecraft: one free server per account, play with friends, no credit card.
- A wide paid game-server catalog beyond Minecraft (Rust, Valheim, ARK, Palworld, CS2, 7 Days to Die, DayZ, Conan Exiles, etc.) — don't invent a specific count of games (a prior pass invented "50+ Games" and had to be corrected — don't repeat that).
- Current promo: first month free on shared hosting plans.
- CTA: "Deploy your server at nxeon.cloud today."

## Real UI references (study these for accurate recreation, don't just screenshot-collage them into TSX — rebuild the layout/chrome/type as real elements per the skill's rules)
`/opt/nxeon/public/blog/screenshots/`: `deploy-wizard.png`, `server-dashboard.png`, `game-servers.png`, `mail-inbox.png`, `ai-builder.png` (Matrix). If you need fresh reference for the free-Minecraft dashboard or admin views, the live site is https://nxeon.cloud — you can WebFetch public marketing pages for visual/copy reference, but the actual portal is behind login, so base your recreation on the screenshots + the brand facts above + your own reasonable judgment for a plausible, on-brand dashboard layout rather than trying to log in.

## The user's own real Minecraft clip (already trimmed, no licensing issue — it's their own footage)
`/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/nxeon-minecraft-clip-4.5s.mp4` — 4.5s, 1920x1080, no audio, h264/mp4, ~3.4MB. Real first-person Minecraft gameplay. Use `baz media upload` for this (check pricing first per the hard rules above — this is likely a free/storage-only operation but verify, don't assume).

## Workflow
```bash
baz project create --name "Nxeon Server Commercial" --json
# or: export BAZ_PROJECT_ID=<id>   (session-scoped, avoids `baz project use` file contention)
baz context add "<goal: ~80s Nxeon commercial recreating the Claude Design Ad motion grammar>" --label goal
baz context add "<brand palette, facts, and hard requirements from above>" --label brand
baz context add "<the adapted 9-beat arc mapped to Nxeon above>" --label instructions
# Author scene TSX files locally, one per beat/repeat, in playback order, then:
baz scenes create --name "<beat name>" --file ./scene.tsx --json
# ...for all ~31 scenes, then fix track/positions in one call:
baz scenes positions --updates-json '<track/start/duration for every scene>' --apply
baz project validate --json
baz preview --frames 0,150,300,450,600,750,900,1050,1200,1350,1500,1650,1800,1950,2100,2250,2400 --json
```
Iterate on any validation errors or bad frames using `baz scenes set-code` (never `baz prompt`). When you're satisfied — STOP. Do not export.

## Report back
File paths of every scene TSX you authored, confirmation `baz project validate` is clean, a description of what the preview frames actually show at several timestamps (so I can sanity-check pacing/content without needing to render it myself), how you handled the Minecraft clip (video-in-tile vs. freeze-frame, and why), any `baz balance --pricing` costs you encountered and stopped for, and total account balance spent (should be $0 — if it's not $0, explain exactly what cost money and why you couldn't avoid it).

63

65	2. Default to a 15-second landscape product launch video unless the request implies another format or duration.

95	- **Direct `baz prompt`** — Scene creation, edits, full agent orchestration

In that workflow, Bazaar is the persistence/review/export control plane, not the code generator.

103	
104	## Phase 1: Context (REQUIRED — do NOT skip)
105	
106	You MUST set project context BEFORE generating any scenes. This gives the composition agent the information it needs to produce correct output on the first try.
107	
108	### Minimum context required:
109	1. **Goal** — What is this video for? Who is the audience? What should they feel/do?
110	2. **Requirements** — Specific, verifiable things the video must contain
111	3. **Brand** — Colors, fonts, logo placement, visual style
112	4. **Director's treatment** — The non-generic creative idea: core metaphor, point of view, pacing shape, visual grammar, and anti-patterns
113	
114	**Shippable quality warning:** "World-class", "premium", "Bloomberg-grade", "cinematic", "editorial", and "not generic" are aspirations, not direction. Do not rely on those words as the prompt. Convert them into a concrete treatment first:
115	
116	- **Core metaphor:** receipt, dossier, pressure gauge, courtroom exhibit, operating-room monitor, teardown, map, timeline, market microstructure, etc.
117	- **Point of view:** the one sentence the video argues, not just the topic it covers.
118	- **Visual grammar:** what kinds of frames repeat, how data is represented, what is deliberately avoided.
119	- **Pacing shape:** where tension rises, where proof lands, where the ending resolves.
120	- **Anti-patterns:** generic KPI cards, interchangeable stock chart panels, decorative data, one-track slideshow pacing, vague finance filler.
121	
122	**Parallel sessions:** If multiple agents share the same machine, do NOT use `baz project use` — it writes to a shared config file and agents will stomp each other. Instead, set the env var for your session:
123	```bash
124	export BAZ_PROJECT_ID=<id>   # Session-scoped, no file contention
125	```

128	# Create or select project
129	baz project create --name "Descriptive Name - Date/Purpose" --json
130	# OR (single-agent only — see parallel sessions note above)
131	baz project use <id>

134	baz context add "Create 45-60 second feature announcement for [Product]. \

145

161	## Phase 2: Generate
162	
163	Now prompt the agent to create scenes. You can use one big prompt or multiple scene-by-scene prompts.
164	
165	```bash
166	# Option A: One comprehensive prompt
167	baz prompt "Create a video with: [scene 1 description], [scene 2], ..." --stream-json
168	
169	# Option B: Scene-by-scene (more control)
170	baz prompt "Scene 1 (5s): Dark gradient intro, logo top-left, title slides up" --stream-json
171	baz prompt "Scene 2 (7s): Problem statement with mock UI..." --stream-json
172	baz prompt "Scene 3 (18s): Feature walkthrough..." --stream-json
173	```
174	
175	Tips:
176	- Include duration in each prompt
177	- Be specific about animations, colors, layout
178	- Reference brand context set in Phase 1

180	### Choreography (REQUIRED for 3+ scene videos)
181	
182	For videos with 3 or more scenes, plan choreography BEFORE generating. This prevents the "lockstep slideshow" pattern where all layers swap at the same frame boundary.
183	
184	#### Actor Planning Template
185	
186	Before prompting, plan your actors:
187	
188	| Actor | Track | Lifetime | Role |
189	|-------|-------|----------|------|
190	| Background | 0 | Full duration | Evolving gradient, particles |
191	| Hero | 1 | 60-80% | Main UI, enters, demotes to corner, returns |
192	| Supporting | 1-2 | 20-40% | Cards/charts, appear during hero demotion |
193	| Text | 2+ | 10-30% | Headlines, arrive at beat points, explicit exits |
194	
195	#### 5 Prompt Enrichment Rules
196	
197	1. **Every content prompt includes exit instructions** (exempt: persistent backgrounds, final CTA)
198	2. **Prefer ONE background** on Track 0 for the full video duration
199	3. **Every overlay prompt includes position and size** — scenes that share screen time must not share screen space
200	4. **Specify spring animation** for hero elements (`spring() for hero entrance`)
201	5. **Include energy level hints** in prompts ("high energy entrance", "calm sustained section")
202	
203	#### Landscape Occupancy Rule (REQUIRED for 16:9)
204	
205	If the project is landscape, do not let the scene collapse into a small claim floating in a giant matte.
206	
207	- Main proof beats should usually use roughly `60-80%` of the frame width, or resolve as a deliberate two-zone composition
208	- Prefer wide proof rails, claim-left / proof-right layouts, split fields, and full-width chart bands
209	- Tiny centered headlines, short decorative lines, or small chart islands are only acceptable as very brief punctuation beats
210	- If a landscape frame feels empty, fix scale and composition first before adding more text
211	
212	#### GOOD Example — context injection + one natural prompt:
213	```bash
214	baz context add "CHOREOGRAPHY: Every overlay scene must specify its position and size. \
215	  Use spring() for hero elements. Every non-final scene must have exit animations. \
216	  Prefer one continuous background. In landscape, main proof beats should occupy roughly 60-80% of width or resolve as a wide split-field layout — avoid tiny centered claim clusters." --label "instructions"
217	
218	baz prompt "Create a 15-second product demo: dark theme intro with logo, \
219	  feature showcase with 3 cards, area chart showing growth, and a CTA. \
220	  Brand: #6366f1 purple, #10b981 green, Inter font." --stream-json

227	## Phase 3: Preview, Review & Validate (REQUIRED — NEVER skip)

229	After generation, you MUST visually inspect the output and run structural validation. This is not optional.

231	### Step 1: Preview
232	```bash
233	baz preview --frames 0,150,300 --json
234	```
235	
236	Use preview for visual and semantic checks:
237	- Is the logo actually visible?
238	- Is the CTA on screen?
239	- Does the style feel on-brand?
240	- Are screenshots being used as reference/recreated UI or charts instead of raw webpage collage?
241	- Are self-claims attributed with small source labels/footers rather than ugly headline copy like "Ramp says..."?
242	- What is the specific visual thesis only this video has?
243	- Could these scenes be reused for any other topic with only text swaps? If yes, fail it.
244	- Are charts and diagrams semantically tied to the story, or just decorative finance motion?
245	- Does the reel feel directed, with a shape and point of view, or like a one-prompt AI slideshow?
246	
247	**Do not accept generic AI slop.** A video can pass validation and still be a 4/10. If the preview reads as generic KPI cards, stock editorial styling, or interchangeable finance graphics, mark it unshippable and return to Phase 1/2 with a stronger treatment. Do not declare done.
248	
249	**Do not accept static infographics.** A still dashboard frame with one glowing line, one receipt/card, and small labels is not a motion-graphics video. Audio timing, word anchors, and a compiled export do not make it shippable. If most preview frames show the same layout with only tiny changes, fail the video as 0-3/10. Require visible choreography: changing composition, object transformations, depth, camera/scale moves, foreground/background interaction, kinetic evidence reveals, and meaningful motion throughout the run.

251	### Step 2: Review
252	```bash
253	baz review --summary --json
254	```
255	
256	Read the project summary. Compare scenes, timing, and context against what Phase 1 asked for.

258	### Step 3: Validate
259	```bash

261	```
262	
263	This is the authoritative machine check for compilation errors, invalid durations, overlaps, and other structural issues.

265	### Optional: Deterministic Verify

269	
270	`baz verify` is now only for deterministic checks like duration, scene count, and format. Do NOT use it for visual/content/style questions.
271	
272	**Gate:** If preview/review reveal problems, or `baz project validate` returns errors, or deterministic `baz verify` fails, you MUST proceed to Phase 4. Do NOT export. Do NOT declare done.
273

276	## Phase 4: Iterate (REQUIRED if Phase 3 fails)
277	
278	Fix the issues. Then re-preview, re-review, and re-validate.

280	```
281	LOOP:
282	  1. Read the visual/content/structural issues from Phase 3
283	  2. Fix with: baz prompt "Fix: [specific issue]" --stream-json
284	  3. Re-run: baz preview --frames 0,150,300 --json
285	  4. Re-run: baz review --summary --json
286	  5. Re-run: baz project validate --json
287	  6. Optional: baz verify --criteria "duration <= 60s,scenes >= 5,portrait" --json
288	  7. If issues remain → GOTO 1
289	  8. If clean enough → proceed to Phase 5
290	```

292	Do NOT exit this loop until the video looks right and structural validation passes.

294	### Deterministic Edits (skip the AI, save tokens)
295	
296	When you know exactly what code change to make — fixing a color, adjusting timing, replacing text, swapping an emoji for an SVG — use `set-code` instead of `baz prompt`. This bypasses the AI agent entirely: you write the code, CLI pushes it to the server. No tokens spent, no prompt randomness.

301	
302	# 2. Edit the file locally (your edits, deterministic)
303	
304	# 3. Push it back

309	- `set-code` — You can see the exact code change needed (wrong color, broken animation, timing fix, text update)
310	- `baz prompt` — You need the AI to design something new or make a creative decision

## ⚠️ Two cost flags you need to know about

**`baz preview` is NOT free — it is `$0.02/call` ("Preview Frame · AWS Lambda").** Your brief listed it as pre-approved free-tier, but the live pricing catalog disagrees. Hard rule #3 says stop for any nonzero cost, so **I did not run `baz preview` at all** (the 17-frame sweep in your workflow would have cost $0.34).

Instead I built a **free local render harness** — esbuild + React 19 SSR + a hand-written shim of Baz's `window.Remotion` API (faithful `interpolate`, `spring`, `Easing`, `AbsoluteFill`, `OffthreadVideo`), screenshotted at true 1920×1080 via the Playwright Chromium already on this box. It renders any scene at any frame for $0, and it caught real bugs (duplicate video tiles, a resizing status pill, a mid-film cursor desync). Every one of the 31 scenes was verified visually this way, plus an automated pass rendering all 31 at start/middle/end: **ALL 31 SCENES RENDER CLEAN**.

Also flagging: **there is no music track**, because music generation is billable (Lyria $0.12/call, Suno $0.50/call) and wasn't pre-approved. The film is cut to a beat grid and is ready for a bed, but the bed isn't there.
